summary: A 1970 note commenting on the Meyer proposal, referring to protocol ideas by another author in the group. It adds feedback from RAND.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 50 records two RAND authors' comments on the Meyer proposal. They favor a simple starting protocol and give views on several features, while noting that some behavior depends on the local installation.

subtitle: RAND's comments on the Meyer proposal and related protocol choices.

tldr.problem: The Meyer proposal raised design choices that needed comments before the network specification was settled.
tldr.mechanism: Harslem and Heafner support the proposal's simplicity and discuss reconnection, interrupts, instance tags, message data types, ASCII, word alignment, queueing and UCC behavior.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records RAND's views and installation-specific comments; it does not state that these views were adopted.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 50 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text records the authors' comments on the Meyer proposal, dated 30 April 1970.

sections.title: Why RAND Supports the Proposal
sections.content: Harslem and Heafner call the Meyer proposal the most acceptable to date because it is simple, sufficient for most planned network uses, easy to implement and extensible. They agree that it does not include every suggested feature, but do not think the missing features justify delaying the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors prefer a simple proposal that can meet most planned needs and be extended later. They do not want to delay a specification to include every proposed feature.

sections.title: Comments on Specific Features
sections.content:
The authors agree that dynamic reconnection may be needed for more advanced uses later, but is unnecessary at first. They support the INT command and an instance-tag subfield so users can distinguish multiple processes when needed. They favor a message data type for transmitted data and support ASCII as a standard character set.

They prefer word-boundary alignment to double padding and accept short-term queueing of requests for comments as an option. They support a standard UCC, while also encouraging parallel experiments, and say the user should not need to know a remote process's socket code.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors support several design choices, including ASCII, instance tags and the INT command. They also argue that a user should not need to know a remote process's socket code to contact it.

sections.title: Flow Control and Local Implementation
sections.content:
The authors say BLK and RSM are more straightforward than earlier suggestions and do not prevent multiplexing over a link. They also say that the ability of a UCC to close connections to a dead process depends on the installation.

At RAND, the NCP is notified directly when a process fails because of the software interface through which all processes, including the NCP, communicate.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors prefer BLK and RSM for their straightforwardness and compatibility with multiplexing. They note that handling a failed process depends on how each installation's software works.

references.text: Meyer, E. E., "ARPA Network Protocol Notes", NWG/RFC 46, 1970.
